whyThisMatters: Real help-desk moments are fast — a ticket, a call, an alert, and you don't always get time to research whether it's genuine. This game trains your reflex for good habits, and helps you catch things that only sound safe.
rememberThis: This month's habit to carry forward: fast instinct is good, but some things only sound safe — a plausible ticket number, a familiar tool's look, a caller who won't wait. When you are not sure, slow down and check before you trust the label.

discussionPrompts: Ask the group which bubble tricked them. Most people get at least one of the trick bubbles wrong on their first try.
Ask why asking a caller for a ticket reference number doesn't actually verify anything.
Ask why taking extra time despite a caller's urgency is listed as a good habit, even though it can feel like making their problem worse.
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: The most common mistake is tapping anything that sounds like part of the job — a plausible ticket number, a tool's familiar look, an urgent caller — without checking the actual sending domain or console. The trick bubbles are there to catch that habit.

bubbles.text: Verified Caller On Approved Contact List
Opened Console Directly Instead Of Alert Link
Opened Remote Access For Unverified Caller
Granted Admin Access From Chat Message
Read Back One-Time Code To Caller

bubbles.note: A second approver is a strong control, but only if that person independently verifies the request rather than approving because someone else already did.

bubbles.text: Took Extra Time Despite Caller's Urgency
bubbles.note: Slowing down when a caller pushes urgency is exactly the right instinct, even though it feels like it's making the caller's problem worse.

bubbles.text: Asked Caller For Ticket Reference Number
bubbles.note: An attacker can invent any reference number that sounds plausible — asking for one feels like a check but doesn't verify anything on its own.

bubbles.text: Followed Instructions From Familiar Tool Style
bubbles.note: A tool's look and branding are easy to copy — a genuine alert never asks for your password through a link, however authentic it looks.
